issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access' directly conflicts with the combination of 'Fragmented Pieces' and repetitive intrusive replay. A patient who says the trauma memory is fragmented and involuntarily replayed would not usually also report being able to talk about it very easily; this is a hard within-node contradiction rather than normal heterogeneity.

issues.item: Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together.
issues.explanation: The maladaptive avoidance items are not clinically well anchored to the rest of the profile or to the military trauma context presented here. Avoiding enclosed spaces and religious spaces suggests specific situational trigger-linked avoidance, but the profile contains no Triggers items and the formulation explicitly leaves Triggers disconnected from the other active components. These avoidance choices therefore do not fit the stated formulation and are hard to connect to the memory/appraisal pattern that is otherwise driving symptoms.

issues.item: Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
issues.explanation: Negative appraisals are generally severe and coherent with high PTSD burden, but because the active formulation centers Negative Appraisals driving Maladaptive Strategies and Memory, the selected maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from those appraisals. 'Screen Escape' fits this, whereas avoidance of enclosed and religious spaces does not clearly follow from the selected appraisals ('Constant Vigilance,' 'Life Not Worth Living,' 'No Accountability').

issues.item: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: The maladaptive avoidance items are not clinically well matched to the rest of the profile or to a military trauma formulation here. Avoiding enclosed spaces and religious spaces suggests highly specific trigger-linked avoidance, but the profile contains no Trigger items and no Threat content tied to confinement, ambush, captivity, worship settings, or comparable trauma cues. This makes these two avoidance items feel disconnected from the reported memory and appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: 'Constant Vigilance' implies an active current-sense-of-threat/hypervigilance presentation. In this formulation, Threat is not active and Negative Appraisals has no link to Threat; the rest of the selected items center more on fragmented/repetitive memory, injustice, hopelessness, and cognitive avoidance. That item therefore sits awkwardly with both the node structure and the absence of any corresponding threat-related content elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: The Negative Appraisals node mixes three quite different themes—ongoing current danger/hypervigilance, severe depressive hopelessness, and moral/injustice-focused appraisal. These can coexist, but with only three appraisal items and no corresponding Threat or Trigger content, the node lacks a clear coherent theme tied to the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: A prominent appraisal of current danger ('Constant Vigilance') would usually connect clinically with Threat and/or Trigger content, but both nodes are absent here and all edges involving Threat/Triggers are inactive. This makes that item poorly aligned with the stated formulation structure.

For a military trauma profile, loud noises are coherent, but alcohol smell and burnt smell together are hard to reconcile clinically without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content indicating fire, explosions, intoxication, barracks/social-drinking contexts, or another olfactory-linked trauma scene. The trigger set implies a specific sensory trauma context that is not represented elsewhere in the profile.

The trigger profile is mostly coherent with military trauma (loud noises, burnt smell), but 'Babies' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type because no memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy item suggests infant-related content or a civilian/family trauma context. This makes that trigger clinically hard to explain within the same trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: 'No Accountability' can occur after military trauma, but here the rest of the profile is dominated by sensory-perceptual trauma memory, generalized danger beliefs, and avoidance/distraction, with no other items indicating moral injury, betrayal, or injustice themes. Given the formulation strongly links Negative Appraisals to Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, this appraisal is insufficiently supported by the accompanying memory and strategy items and sits apart from the otherwise fear-based profile.

The trigger items are strongly combat-specific and plausibly fit military trauma, but the formulation marks all Triggers pathways as inactive, including Triggers → Threat, Triggers → Memory, and Triggers → Negative Appraisals. With three intense sensory trauma reminders selected, one would expect at least some linked threat or memory activation. As written, the trigger node is too active and trauma-specific to sit coherently as an isolated component in this formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The appraisal items 'World is Dangerous' and 'I have to be on guard all the time' imply a persistent sense of current threat, yet Threat is entirely disconnected in the formulation and no Threat items are present. These appraisals can occur in PTSD, but together they function as threat-laden beliefs that sit awkwardly with a model where Negative Appraisals link mainly to Memory and Maladaptive Strategies rather than to current threat processing.

vignette:
At just 21 years old, Marcus found himself grappling with the shadows of his past, a past shaped by his service in the military. The chaos of war had left indelible marks on his psyche, and as he sat in the driver’s seat of the bus he operated daily, he often thought back to the day when everything changed. It was in a distant land, under a scorching sun, where an explosion had rocked his world. The memory of that day was a jumbled collection of images—he could see flashes of light, hear screams, and feel the heat of the blast—but they came to him in disjointed fragments that refused to align into a coherent narrative. The scene replayed in his mind like a relentless film, each viewing stirring up a cocktail of dread and despair that he struggled to articulate.

The aftermath of that traumatic event had shifted Marcus's perceptions fundamentally. The belief that he was fundamentally broken led him to ruminate on the events of that day, making the memories of the explosion sharper and more distressing, as if he were reliving the moment of his failure repeatedly. This negative appraisal contributed to his decision to avoid confronting those memories, as he believed that facing them would only reinforce his sense of being broken and unworthy. Marcus had come to view his memories as a relentless source of pain, leading him to develop strategies like isolating himself to prevent any chance of triggering those painful recollections, believing that avoidance was his only means of self-preservation. He began to see the world as a perilous place, filled with unseen threats lurking around every corner. This belief reinforced his decision to stay home, as he felt that venturing outside would only expose him to more danger; it seemed the only logical choice in a world where he perceived himself as vulnerable. This pervasive sense of danger seeped into his daily life, convincing him that he had to remain constantly vigilant. His negative appraisals led him to think that seeking help or reaching out to others would only expose him to further harm, solidifying his retreat into isolation. He feared that any loud noise might trigger a flashback, so he avoided crowded places where sounds could easily overwhelm him. This fear of being overwhelmed by memories led him to convince himself that staying away from such environments was the only logical choice, as he believed exposing himself to triggers would only solidify his feelings of inadequacy. Shopping centers became no-go zones; the clamor of voices mixed with the clanging of carts felt like a cacophony of potential threats. Likewise, he found himself steering clear of religious spaces, where the sense of community and worship was overshadowed by the anxiety of being in a crowd. With these fears taking hold, Marcus turned to his phone, spending long hours immersed in games and the internet. This distraction became a way to escape from the painful thoughts that clawed at him, a temporary reprieve from the reality of his life, where he often questioned whether life was even worth living.

As the weeks turned into months, this cycle deepened. The avoidance behaviors he adopted to escape his feelings also served to entrench them, as the more he distanced himself from reality, the more fragmented his memories became. The memories, once vivid, now felt like distant echoes, slipping through his fingers just as he tried to grasp them. Each time he attempted to recall the events, they would surge back with a haunting intensity, reinforcing his belief that he was irreparably damaged and unworthy of happiness. In response to this overwhelming sensation, Marcus found himself increasingly retreating into his phone and online games, believing that distraction would shield him from the distressing thoughts that threatened to resurface. To manage the overwhelming nature of these memories, Marcus found himself increasingly retreating into his phone and online games, believing that distraction would shield him from the distressing thoughts that threatened to resurface. He had learned that if he kept himself occupied with games, he could momentarily escape the vivid memories of the explosion that haunted him, but this avoidance only made those memories more potent whenever they surfaced. By avoiding any confrontation with those memories, he inadvertently kept them intact and undisturbed, ensuring that they remained as vivid and distressing as ever. He had come to believe that if he avoided confronting those memories, he could stave off the inevitable pain that accompanied them, thinking it was better to remain numb than to face the truth of his suffering. He would sit in silence, knowing he had experienced something horrific but unable to find the words to describe it, leaving him feeling isolated in his suffering. The longer he avoided confronting the memories, the more they remained intact and undisturbed, lurking in the background of his mind, waiting to reemerge with an intensity that took him by surprise. The weight of these memories fed into his negative appraisals, reinforcing his belief that his life had little value. Each flashback that surged forth carried with it a haunting reminder of his perceived failures, leading Marcus to conclude that he was fundamentally broken and unworthy of happiness. This conviction kept him from seeking out social connections, as he feared that sharing his experiences would only confirm the belief that he was unworthy of support or understanding. Each time a helicopter flew overhead or an explosion was heard in the distance—whether it was from a movie or a construction site—it triggered a panic that would send him spiraling. Those moments were like a cruel reminder of his past, causing him to retreat further into his digital worlds, away from the harshness of reality.

Despite the soothing glow of his phone screen, Marcus was aware that these maladaptive strategies were a double-edged sword. They provided a temporary escape but also compounded his struggles. The more he avoided the world, the more entrenched his negative thoughts became. Each act of avoidance, though initially providing relief, only solidified his negative appraisals, leading him to believe that engaging with life would inevitably result in further pain and suffering. He felt stuck in a loop, where the fragmented memories of trauma fed into his belief that he could never find peace, and in turn, those beliefs propelled him deeper into avoidance. He longed to regain control over his life, yet each attempt to confront his feelings felt like an insurmountable task, pushing him back into a cycle of despair.

It was during a quiet moment of reflection, sitting in his bus after a long shift, that the reality of his situation struck him. He could no longer ignore the toll his experiences were taking on his life. The weight of his memories, the constant hypervigilance, and the overwhelming sense of danger that colored every aspect of his existence had become unbearable. He realized that he needed help to break free from the grip of his trauma, to redefine his relationship with the world outside and within. As he contemplated reaching out for support, he felt a flicker of hope mixed with dread. He was terrified of what the journey might entail, yet he also yearned for a life where he could once again feel safe and, perhaps, even find meaning. With this realization, Marcus resolved to seek help, understanding that change was possible, but it would require confronting the very memories he had tried so hard to escape.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not convey how negative appraisals influence the use of maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."

  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
